title: Being an Entrepreneur Linked to Longer Lifespan
paragraphs: Running your own business often means long hours, financial uncertainty and plenty of stress. But perhaps surprisingly, it may also be linked to a longer life.
A new study of more than 27,000 older Americans found that people with entrepreneurial experience had about a 10% lower risk of death than those who worked for someone else.

The study, published in the Journal of Business Venturing, used data from the US Health and Retirement Study, which followed adults aged 50 and over between 1998 and 2020. Even after things like age, earnings and past health problems were considered, the link between entrepreneurship and lower risk of death remained.
So what might be behind it?
One possible explanation is the greater control that comes with running your own business.

"Most people think of entrepreneurship as extremely stressful, and it certainly can be," said study author Cristiano Bellavitis. "But entrepreneurship also gives people a high degree of autonomy and the opportunity to pursue something they genuinely love or care about. Our findings suggest those benefits may have lasting effects."
The study also found that entrepreneurs had better mental health, including lower levels of depression and loneliness.
But not all entrepreneurs benefited equally.

The positive link with lifespan was concentrated among so-called "opportunity-driven" entrepreneurs — people who wanted to leave their regular job and go into self-employment. Those who entered self-employment after losing a job did not show the same advantage.
Also, the longer people were involved in entrepreneurship, the stronger the link with longer lifespan was.

Still, that doesn't mean everyone should quit their job and start a company, Bellavitis said. Traditional workplaces could offer some of the same benefits by giving employees more control and ownership over their work — while still offering the security of regular employment.
